EXPLORER 1 · LESSON 5

Animals & Everyday Objects for Babies 6–9 Months

Age 6–9 MonthsSubject Talk & ThinkClass Baby 1Duration 3–5 minutes

Around six to nine months, babies reach for what interests them, light up at familiar pictures and love a funny animal sound. This class pairs twelve realistic animals with everyday objects — a cat, a dog, a bird, a fish, a duck, a cow, then a ball, a shoe, a cup, a spoon, a car and a teddy bear — shown one at a time while you name what you see and play with simple sounds.

There is no script and nothing to test. Your baby looks and listens, you talk and play, and every little connection — woof, moo, ball, cup — grows early recognition at your baby’s own pace. Short, playful sessions of three to five minutes are all it takes.

Start Today’s Class ↓Twelve cards, one at a time. Name each picture and add an animal sound if you like — short and playful wins.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use this activity

Sit with your baby when they are awake and comfortable. Show one card at a time and clearly name what you see. Keep your language simple: ‘cat’, ‘dog’, ‘ball’ or ‘Here is the cup.’

For animals, you can also make a simple sound such as ‘woof’ or ‘moo’. For everyday objects, point out the real object later when you see it together.

Give your baby time to look, listen and respond in their own way. There is no need to ask them to identify or name the pictures.

Keep the activity short and stop when your baby loses interest.

Every baby develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

TRY TOGETHER

Little things to say.

Prompts for you, not for the cards — say them softly while your baby looks.

  • Dog. Woof woof!
  • Look, a bird.
  • Here is the ball.
  • That’s a cup.
  • Can you see the cow? Moo!
REAL-WORLD CONNECTION

Find It in Real Life

Learning can continue away from the screen. When you see one of these animals or objects during your day, point it out and name it naturally.

  • See a dog → “Dog!”
  • Hold baby’s cup → “Your cup.”
  • Pick up a shoe → “Shoe.”
  • See a bird outside → “Bird!”

    Cat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The Baby 1 stage begins here, with the friendliest animal in the set. This lesson builds the rhythm that carries all six animal cards: tap, name, sound, wait — and whatever comes back is conversation.

    What is this?

    A cat is a small, soft, whiskered animal that naps, prowls and says meow. At 6–9 months your baby is ready for the full animal experience: the picture, the name, the sound, and — arriving soon — a pointing finger of their own.

    What does it mean?

    Animal words are vocabulary with the volume turned up: each arrives with motion, noise and drama attached. The meow is the hook, but the deeper work is the turn-taking — you say your bit, the silence opens, and your baby discovers they have a side in this.

    What does the child need to know?

    The rhythm is the whole method: tap the picture, say the word, make the sound, then hold a real silence. A squeal, a babble, a bounce or a stare — anything back is your baby’s turn. And if a real cat appears this week, one word more makes the set permanent.

    Why this matters

    Sounds are the easiest door into language for this stage: before babies manage words, they can manage noises, and meow is nearly a noise by itself. Every animal conversation now is rehearsal for every conversation later — someone speaks, someone answers.

    What it teaches

    Animal recognition, sound imitation attempts, turn-taking in “conversation”, and the emerging gesture system — reaching, tapping and the first backward-point at pictures.

    Words to learn

    catmeowsoftearswhiskersagain

    Say this to your child

    ““Cat! Here is the cat, with its pointy ears and long whiskers. A cat says meow — meow! Such a soft little sound. Can you hear it? Meow. Your turn now, little one. Tell the cat something.””

    Step by step

    1. Sit your baby supported on your lap and bring the card to just beyond arm’s length — close enough to study, far enough to tap.
    2. Tap the cat gently and say its name: “Cat.” Then the sound: “Meow” — soft, rising, twice at most.
    3. Open a real silence and count to five inside your head; every squeak, kick or babble in that gap is your baby’s reply.
    4. Answer the reply warmly — “yes! meow!” — and run the rhythm once more if interest holds.
    5. If a hand comes towards the card, let it land and smooth the picture with their fingers; touching the cat is part of knowing it.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a soft, watchy cat in realistic detail — the ears, the whiskers, the watching eyes. Say what you see, then move the noticing forward: in the silence after your meow, what does your baby do? That gap is where the conversation either starts or does not.

    Ask your child

    Watch the turn: does your baby answer sounds now with sounds of their own? Does a finger hover over the picture? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you are storing meow somewhere — it sounds like it.”

    What your child can say or do

    A squeal or rasp aimed back at your meow, fingers stroking the picture, a bounce of the whole body at the sound, or a first wobbly point at the cat — pointing at what you mean is the biggest news of this stage, and it starts exactly like this.

    Out in the real world

    Cats prowl through the week: over the fence, through a book, on a friend’s jumper. Each appearance takes the one-word replay — “cat!” — and the sound if your baby’s mood invites it. Real cats are the best advertising this card could ask for.

    Try it together

    Sound tennis: meow to your baby, wait, answer whatever returns, wait again. Three or four exchanges is a full match. You are not teaching the sound — you are teaching the game where sounds go back and forth, which is the game talking is built on.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you leave at least one honest five-second silence, and did your baby get to “say” anything back? The silence is the gift; without it, animal sounds become a lecture instead of a chat.

    Parent tips

    Keep sounds below their startling threshold — soft meows breed confidence, loud ones breed caution. If your baby points at the cat, answer the pointing with the word instantly; the gesture-and-name link you build now feeds every word after.

    Staying safe

    Real cats stay the authors of their own participation: supervised glimpses, never forced contact, claws and food bowls out of the story. Card sessions stay on your lap — at this age, silence plus paper plus a hand equals chewing.

    This lesson pairs with the Cat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Dogs perform themselves: the sound is famous, the wag is famous, and the baby version of both is arriving right about now. This lesson stages the dog card as a two-part act.

    What is this?

    A dog is a four-legged friend that barks, wags and adores outings — and it is the animal your baby is likeliest to meet in the flesh. The card gives a clear portrait; your woof and your floppy-ear hands give it a performance your baby can join.

    What does it mean?

    Two channels are better than one: a word with a sound and an action offers your baby two roads in. Some babies answer sounds first, some answer movement, and a few manage both — whichever road your baby takes, the word waits at the end of it.

    What does the child need to know?

    The act is simple: the woof, then the ear-flap hands, then silence. And across the week, say the word about every dog there is — enormous, tiny, loud, asleep — because at this stage your baby is learning that one name covers a whole population of very different animals.

    Why this matters

    Dog is often the first animal word a child owns outright, because dogs supply so many rehearsals: on walks, in books, behind fences, on the telly. Owning the word turns every future dog into a named event — and named events are how a baby’s world gets organised.

    What it teaches

    Sound recognition and imitation, action imitation (the copy-me wave of the next stage starts here), generalisation across different-looking examples, and reaction-and-recovery to sudden noises.

    Words to learn

    dogwoofwagearsbigsmall

    Say this to your child

    ““Dog! A great big happy dog, tongue out, tail going. A dog says woof! Woof, woof! And look — my hands are floppy ears. Big dogs say woof, small dogs say woof, sleepy dogs say woof. Everyone knows this word by heart.””

    Step by step

    1. Bring the card to viewing distance and greet it: “Dog! Look at that happy face.”
    2. Tap the tail and give it a wiggle with your fingertip — the wag is the dog’s signature, and yours to perform.
    3. Do the woof — two short friendly ones — then pat your own head like floppy ears while your baby watches.
    4. Hold the silence open. A laugh, a kick, a babble that sounds like a reply: answer all of it with delight.
    5. Across the week, replay the word at every dog you meet — the giant one, the yappy one, the sleeping one — same word, every size.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a happy dog with its tongue out and tail mid-wag — say that much. The live noticing: which part of the act does your baby copy — the sound, the hand-movement, or neither yet? Imitation at this stage is a coin with two faces, and either face counts.

    Ask your child

    Watch the copying: does a hand wave after your ear-flaps? Does a sound follow your woof? Wonder aloud: “I wonder which of us is training which — you have me doing this dog three times a day.”

    What your child can say or do

    A babbled burst right after the woof, arms that flap when yours do, a full-leg jiggle of joy, or a solemn stare that saves its reaction for the third round — copy-me behaviour at 6–9 months rarely fires on the first performance, so keep the act in rotation.

    Out in the real world

    Dogs are everywhere once you start counting: the neighbour’s behind the gate, the one asleep outside the café, every other page of the animal book. Each is a replay of word, sound and — if your hands are free — ears.

    Try it together

    Woof-and-freeze: do the woof, then go completely still with an expectant face. The stillness is the invitation; whatever noise or movement your baby loads into it, celebrate like it was a word. Because functionally, it was.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word cover more than one dog this week, and did the act get a silence at the end for your baby’s half? The variety teaches the generalisation; the silence teaches the conversation.

    Parent tips

    Commit to the performance — an apologetic woof teaches half a word. If your baby startles hard at the sound, drop the volume and keep the ears; some babies take the visual road first and find the sound later. Both roads are open.

    Staying safe

    Real dogs are met only on their owner’s terms and at a safe distance — the card carries the lesson and the fence carries the dog. Watch reaction-and-recovery: a startle that settles fast is healthy; a baby who cannot settle needs the quiet version of this card.

    This lesson pairs with the Dog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    Bird — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Birds catch baby eyes before any other wild creature: they move fast, they move often, and they move for free outside every window. This lesson attaches their name to the show.

    What is this?

    A bird is a small feathered animal that flies, hops and cheeps. The card holds one still; the window cannot hold one at all — and that difference is exactly what makes the word worth learning from both.

    What does it mean?

    Bird comes pre-loaded with motion, and motion is what this stage’s eyes are built to catch. Naming a bird at the moment it moves welds the word to the event — the strongest kind of vocabulary there is, because the thing and the name arrive together.

    What does the child need to know?

    The method runs in two places: the card for the clear portrait, then the window for the live show. One real bird, named once as it flies, outweighs any number of rounds at the card. Birds also sing — the tweet is yours to add, and it belongs to the card session.

    Why this matters

    Window words are a baby’s first reach beyond the grabbable world: birds, sun, cars, trees — things too far away to hold. Learning bird means learning that language covers the out-there, which quietly changes what all future looking is for.

    What it teaches

    Motion tracking at distance, word-event association, sound exposure through the tweet, and shared attention — the two of you watching one small event and both knowing it.

    Words to learn

    birdflytweetwingsskyquick

    Say this to your child

    ““Bird! Here is the picture bird — wings ready, tail out. A bird goes tweet, tweet! And now look outside... up on the branch, across the sky. Birds fly out there, fast as thoughts. When you see one, that is the bird word.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at viewing distance and name it: “Bird! A little bird with quick wings.”
    2. Trace the wing and flap your hand gently — birds are essentially their flying.
    3. Add the tweet: two light rising notes, nothing loud. Then a beat of quiet for your baby’s side.
    4. Move to the window, baby settled against you, and watch together without narrating — the quiet is the stage.
    5. The moment a bird moves, say “bird” once. One word per event; the restraint is what keeps the word rare and valuable.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bright little bird in bold simple shape — say that much. The live noticing: what does your baby track at the window — birds, leaves, light? Name what they actually follow, not what the lesson hoped for; honesty is what makes noticing real.

    Ask your child

    Watch the window: does a flying bird beat a still branch for attention? Does the word alone, said indoors later, earn a glance towards the glass? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you would point at the next one — your finger is getting opinionated lately.”

    What your child can say or do

    A locked stare on the flying bird, a squeal as it goes, both hands rising towards the glass, or a finger that half-extends towards the branch — the half-point is the milestone in progress, and naming what it aims at is how it finishes forming.

    Out in the real world

    Birds are the cheapest wild show on earth: the lawn, the wire, the car park, the feeder. One word per sighting, forever — this card pays out for years, and the payout starts the day you learn to wait quietly at glass.

    Try it together

    Wing-echo: at the card, flap your hands and lift them as you say “fly”. Your baby cannot copy it yet — but the motion-word pair sinks in, and one random Tuesday a flapping baby will prove it landed. That Tuesday is worth the wait.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the session actually reach the window, and did you manage one-word-per-bird instead of a running commentary? Scarcity is what makes naming work; narrate everything and the word drowns in the narration.

    Parent tips

    No birds today? The window still teaches, and the card still holds. Learn your house’s bird hour — most have one — and hold that slot for this lesson. If your baby points at anything out there, that thing gets the word, bird or not.

    Staying safe

    Window watching happens against your body or a supported seat, never propped at the glass; latches stay locked if small hands are near. Balconies and open sashes are adult territory — the lesson ends where the pane begins.

    This lesson pairs with the Bird flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    Fish — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Every animal set needs a calm card, and the fish is it — no barking, no flapping, just a serene swimmer with a mouth that opens and closes like a tiny joke. This lesson plays the mouth.

    What is this?

    A fish is a swimming animal with fins, scales and a famously round, gulping mouth. The card gives a clear, friendly portrait; your face gives the performance; and 6–9-month babies are the perfect audience, because they study mouths for a living.

    What does it mean?

    Babies at this stage watch mouths intensely — it is where words come from, and they are quietly taking notes. A fish face is mouth-theatre: the opening and closing gives your baby exactly the movement their own mouth is practising, wearing a funny costume.

    What does the child need to know?

    Make the fish face — lips pushed out, opening and closing slowly — and add a soft “glub” if the mood allows. Then wait. If there is an aquarium or even a fish picture anywhere in your world, that is the word’s real twin; visit it within the week.

    Why this matters

    Fish is a quiet word with a hidden curriculum: mouth-play builds the exact muscles and attention that babbling runs on. And as the calm card in a loud set, it teaches range — sounds can be big like woof or small like glub, and language owns both.

    What it teaches

    Mouth-movement watching (pre-speech work), imitation of facial play, sound-volume range from quiet to loud, and animal recognition in the water category.

    Words to learn

    fishglubswimbubblesmouthquiet

    Say this to your child

    ““Fish! Here is the fish, gliding through the water, quiet as a bubble. Look at its little mouth — open, and closed, and open. Glub! Can you see? Fish never make a fuss. Fish just swim, and their mouths do this all day.””

    Step by step

    1. Lift the card into view and keep your voice low: “Fish — a quiet fish, swimming along.”
    2. Trace the fin and the round mouth with your fingertip — the mouth is the star, so visit it last.
    3. Make the fish face at your baby: lips out, opening and closing in slow motion. Hold it longer than feels dignified.
    4. Add one soft “glub”, then stop and watch. Some babies freeze, some grin, some try a mouth-shape back.
    5. Close with a second slow fish face and the word once more — this card should feel like a whisper between the loud animal cards.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a round, friendly fish with its mouth visible — say that much. The live noticing: during the fish face, where are your baby’s eyes — your mouth, the card’s mouth, their own hands? Mouth-watching at your face is pre-speech behaviour happening in real time.

    Ask your child

    Watch the mouth-work: does your baby study your lips, or the card’s? Do they try a mouth-shape back, or a rasp of a sound? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you know your mouth and mine are doing the same trick.”

    What your child can say or do

    A fixed stare at your working lips, a slow grin mid-face, a babble that rises right after the glub, or a hand that pats the card’s mouth — and sometimes, weeks later out of nowhere, a fish face of their own. That one is worth the whole set.

    Out in the real world

    Fish live in frames and tanks: the aquarium at the dentist, the goldfish bowl at grandma’s, the fish on the bath thermometer. Any real fish, named once, anchors the word — and bath time offers fish-shaped toys as understudies.

    Try it together

    Bubble voice: make a gentle b-b-b-b sound with closed lips — motorboat style — as you trace a swimming path with the card through the air. Sound plus motion plus mouth-play, all quiet, all silly, all repeatable at bath or mat time.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you hold the fish face long enough to feel silly, and did the session stay quiet from start to finish? The silliness is the bait; the quiet is the lesson. Both, or neither.

    Parent tips

    This is the breather card — slot it between dog and duck rather than opening with it. If your baby is fractious, fish faces work almost like a reset: slow mouths calm fast babies more reliably than shushing does.

    Staying safe

    Water-zone versions of this card — aquarium visits, bath toys — keep hands outside glass and toys inside supervision. And keep the glub small: this card’s job is contrast, and a shouted glub is just another woof.

    This lesson pairs with the Fish flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    Duck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The duck arrives with everything included: a sound babies can almost make, a walk everyone can mock, and a bath-toy twin already floating in most homes. This lesson lets the comedy lead.

    What is this?

    A duck is a water bird that quacks, waddles and paddles — practically a ready-made game. The card gives the cheerful portrait; your hand does the waddle; and somewhere in the house, most weeks, a rubber duck confirms everything.

    What does it mean?

    Physical comedy lands hard at this stage: unexpected movement makes babies laugh before any joke does. The waddling hand across the card is funny the first time and funnier the fifth — and every laugh attaches the word to a moment your baby enjoyed being alive in.

    What does the child need to know?

    Quack twice, waddle your hand across the card, and let the laughter finish before you go again. Comedy needs rhythm: sound, waddle, pause, repeat. And the bath-twin is this card’s secret weapon — a real duck-duck at bathtime ties the word to the happiest room in the house.

    Why this matters

    Laughter is a memory glue at every age, and at 6–9 months it is free. A word learned in giggles gets recalled with a smile — duck is the set’s word-your-baby-will-grin-at, and that association is worth more than any drill.

    What it teaches

    Sound imitation attempts (quack is wonderfully plosive), anticipation of repeated jokes, cause-and-effect joy (I laugh, the duck goes again), and animal recognition in the water-bird family.

    Words to learn

    duckquackwaddlewatersplashfunny

    Say this to your child

    ““Duck! Look at this cheerful duck, standing by the water. A duck says quack! Quack, quack! And here it goes — waddle, waddle, waddle, all the way across. Ducks walk like tiny sailors. Isn’t that the funniest thing you ever saw?””

    Step by step

    1. Bring the card up and announce it brightly: “Duck! A cheerful duck, ready to waddle.”
    2. Do the quack — two crisp ones — and watch your baby’s face rather than the card.
    3. Now the waddle: walk two fingers slowly across the card’s surface, beak to tail, tipping side to side.
    4. Pause. Laughter, kicks, a reaching hand — whatever lands, answer it, then run the act once more if invited.
    5. At the next bath, hand over or float the rubber duck with the same word — the card’s joke, performed live by the bathroom cast.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a cheerful duck — bright bill, round body, pond behind it. Say what you see. The live noticing: does the waddling hand earn more than the quack, or the other way round? Your baby is telling you whether they are an ears-first or eyes-first learner this month.

    Ask your child

    Watch the rhythm: does the anticipation build by the second round — eyes going to the card before the quack arrives? Wonder aloud: “I wonder when the joke became predictable to you — and whether predictable is the part you love.”

    What your child can say or do

    Big open-mouth laughter at the waddle, a reaching grab for the walking fingers, babble that tries the k-sound after quack, or a bath-time excitement that starts at the word alone — the last one means the joke has left the card and moved into the bathroom.

    Out in the real world

    Ducks live in parks, ponds, books and baths. The park version — real, noisy, bread-free — is the deluxe replay; the bath version is the daily one. Both take the same word, and the word gets stronger every time.

    Try it together

    Bath duck theatre: at bath time, make the rubber duck quack and waddle across the water’s edge, then under a washcloth — duck gone! — and back out. Object permanence, animal vocabulary and comedy in one small splashy show.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you wait for the laugh before repeating the joke, and did the rubber duck get its word at bath time too? The laugh-gap and the bath-twin are this card’s two engines — run both and the word flies.

    Parent tips

    If the quack delights and the waddle baffles, drop the waddle; the animal lesson survives on sound alone. Keep the act identical across days — babies love jokes they can predict, and predictability is what turns comedy into ritual.

    Staying safe

    Bath versions happen inside normal bath supervision — one hand on the baby at all times, ducks in the water not the mouth. Park duck-watching happens from the pushchair, at a respectful duck-distance; real water birds are admirers-only.

    This lesson pairs with the Duck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    Cow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Every animal card has its gimmick, and the cow’s is endurance: one note, held long, getting funnier the longer it goes. This lesson teaches the word through stamina.

    What is this?

    A cow is a big, calm farm animal that eats grass and says moo — a sound with no sharp edges, no speed, just length. The card gives the gentle giant’s portrait; your lungs give the performance.

    What does it mean?

    Long sounds are wonderfully funny at this stage, and they are also ear-training: hearing one sound stretch and change teaches your baby to listen inside a sound — where it starts, how it wobbles, when it ends. That listening is the raw material of every word they will ever hear.

    What does the child need to know?

    Hold the moo for as long as your baby stays interested — that is the whole technique. Not loud, just long, with a small wobble in the middle for comedy. When the sound ends, stop everything; the silence after a long moo is practically a standing ovation.

    Why this matters

    Before babies speak, they listen — and listening is a trainable skill, not a given. Cow trains it at maximum fun: a sound that long cannot be ignored, and babies who track a moo from start to finish are doing genuine phonological work while thinking they are watching a cow.

    What it teaches

    Auditory attention and sound-tracking, length discrimination (short sounds versus long ones), big-and-gentle animal concepts, and shared silliness that keeps learning warm.

    Words to learn

    cowmoolongbiggrassgentle

    Say this to your child

    ““Cow! A big cow, standing so still in the grass. And a cow says... moooooooooo! Just one long sound, going and going. Such a big animal, such a slow sound. Moooo... all done. Did you hear how long that was? The cow was not in a hurry at all.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at viewing distance and set the scene: “Cow! A big, gentle cow, standing in the grass.”
    2. Trace the cow’s broad back and gentle face — this animal is mostly calm, and the card should feel calm too.
    3. Take a breath and deliver the moo: long, low, with one little wobble halfway. Keep it going while your baby keeps listening.
    4. Stop the moment attention breaks — the first look-away ends the note, always. Then enjoy the quiet together.
    5. Run the moo once more later in the session, slightly shorter; the repeat is the part they will start anticipating.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a big, gentle cow — broad body, calm face, grass at its feet. Say that much. The live noticing: how long does your baby track the moo — and is today’s record longer than yesterday’s? That creeping number is real auditory growth you can chart in seconds.

    Ask your child

    Watch the listening: does your baby still before the sound or during it? Do they look startled when the moo finally ends? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you like the beginning of the moo or the wobble in the middle — the wobble is my favourite too.”

    What your child can say or do

    Whole-body stilling at the long note, mouth movements that echo the moo’s shape, a startle-laugh when it ends, or babble that tries an open ah-sound afterwards — the moo’s vowel is one your baby’s mouth is already fishing for, and hearing it stretched helps.

    Out in the real world

    Cows graze in picture books, on farm toys, out of train windows and in the fields of every car journey ever taken. Each sighting is a moo waiting to happen — and few words offer this much fun per syllable.

    Try it together

    Long-and-short: do the long moo, then a tiny “moo!” like a sneeze, then ask yourself aloud which was longer while tapping the card for the long one. You are not testing your baby — you are modelling comparison, out loud, with a cow.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the moo actually run long today, and did it end the moment interest did? The discipline of ending on the first look-away is what keeps this card welcome — push past it and the whole note turns to noise.

    Parent tips

    If you feel ridiculous, good — ridiculous is the working state of baby classes. Vary the wobble’s position across days; regulars get anticipatory grins. And if your baby starts mooing back in babble-form, that is imitation’s first draft: celebrate it loudly.

    Staying safe

    Volume stays conversational — long does not mean loud, and a baby’s ears get one childhood. Farm toys and cow books are fine backups; real cows are met at gates and over fences, always on the animal’s side of them.

    This lesson pairs with the Cow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

    Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The animal cards end and the everyday half of the set begins — with the object your baby has probably already pushed, dropped and chased across a kitchen floor. This lesson names all of that.

    What is this?

    A ball is a round toy that rolls, bounces and falls — and at 6–9 months your baby is deep in a research programme about exactly those properties. The card gives the portrait; your floor supplies the laboratory.

    What does it mean?

    Dropping things off the high chair is not mischief at this age — it is physics: what happens when I let go? Naming the ball through all its experiments gives the science a vocabulary. The word travels with the object through every fall and retrieval.

    What does the child need to know?

    Roll the ball towards your baby and name it as it moves — action words love moving objects. Then let your baby’s own version happen: the push, the drop, the tumble off the tray. Each one gets the same calm word, and the game becomes vocabulary practice wearing mischief’s clothes.

    Why this matters

    Balls teach the physical world’s first big rules — things move, things fall, things come back. A baby with the word ball can carry those rules in their head: name it, drop it, watch it, name it again. Language turns play into knowledge you can keep.

    What it teaches

    Object permanence in action (the ball exists even under the chair), cause-and-effect experimentation, tracking in two directions, and action-naming — words attached to movement rather than stillness.

    Words to learn

    ballrolldroppushgoneback again

    Say this to your child

    ““Ball! Watch it roll — all the way to you. And back it goes. Push it! There it goes — and stop. Dropped it? Ball goes down, down... and here I come to fetch it. Round things love to travel. Ball is the word for all of it.””

    Step by step

    1. Settle your baby and show the card: “Ball! Round, bright, and always up to something.”
    2. Roll a real ball slowly towards them, saying “ball” as it moves, and let their hands stop it.
    3. Roll it back the other way — tracking both directions is a new skill this stage — and name it again, once.
    4. If your baby pushes or drops the ball, narrate the fall warmly: “ball — gone! ... there it is.” No scolding; the physics is the point.
    5. Close with the card again, and let the ball live where your baby can find it for the rest of the day.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bright, bouncy ball — say that much. The live noticing: which ball event collects the most attention — the roll towards, the roll away, or the drop? Your baby’s preference is a window into what their brain is currently solving for.

    Ask your child

    Watch the experiments: does your baby push the ball deliberately, with eyes on its path? Do they look to you after the drop — checking whether you saw? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you dropped it to see me fetch it. I suspect you did, you little scientist.”

    What your child can say or do

    A two-handed push with total focus, head-tracking the roll in both directions, the classic tray-drop with immediate eye-contact to you, or delighted squeals at the return — every version is an experiment, and your narration is the lab report.

    Out in the real world

    Balls fill the months ahead: the soft one in the cot, the big one at baby group, every ball that ever rolls under the sofa. Each one runs the same curriculum — and by toddlerhood, your child will supply the word themselves, in the middle of the game.

    Try it together

    Under-the-blanket ball: roll the ball behind a cushion, pause, then bring it back with “there it is!” This is object permanence — gone is not gone — staged with the exact object your baby most suspects of magic.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the ball roll in both directions today, and did the drops get words instead of sighs? Accepting the drop as curriculum is the hardest part of this lesson and the most important — physics does not negotiate.

    Parent tips

    Keep the ball big enough to defeat swallowing and light enough to fail at hurting. If your baby is in a drop-everything phase, this card is your best friend: the phase is not a bug, it is the lesson running at full speed.

    Staying safe

    Ball choice follows the fist rule — bigger than theirs, no seams splitting, no foam crumbs. High-chair play stays supervised and strapped; the game is dropping the ball, never diving after it.

    This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

    Shoe — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Some words come with their own schedule, and shoe is the best example: it shows up at every doorway, twice, forever. This lesson attaches the card to the routine that never stops.

    What is this?

    A shoe is a foot covering that marks the border between home and world — shoes off inside, shoes on outside, all day, every day. Your baby has watched this ritual since birth; the card gives it a picture and a name.

    What does it mean?

    Routine words are the highest-frequency words in a baby’s life: they repeat not because you drill them but because the day does. Shoe arrives at predictable moments — the mat, the door, the pushchair — and predictability is what makes words stick.

    What does the child need to know?

    The twin moment happens at the next doorway: touch a real shoe as it goes on and say the word once. No lesson-drama needed — the routine is the lesson. Your baby will hear shoe dozens of times a week anyway; the card just makes sure the word has a face.

    Why this matters

    Learning the words of routines gives a baby a map of the day: shoe means going out, bath means water, cup means milk. That map is early security — a baby who can read the day’s signals fights its transitions less. Few cards buy this much calm per word.

    What it teaches

    Routine recognition, word-event association at real transitions, anticipation (shoes mean outside), and the body-awareness seed that shoe connects to foot.

    Words to learn

    shoeonoffsocktoesoutside

    Say this to your child

    ““Shoe! Here is the picture shoe. And look — here is your little foot, with its sock. Shoes go over socks, and shoes mean outside. Shoe on — we are going somewhere! Shoe off — we are home. What a useful word to know.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at a calm moment: “Shoe! Shoes go on, shoes come off — all day long.”
    2. Trace the sole and the laces or strap, naming the parts as your finger goes.
    3. Hold the card near your baby’s own feet, then touch their sock — the card-to-body link is the quiet centre of this lesson.
    4. At the next doorway, touch the real shoe as it goes on: “shoe.” Same word, same calm, no fuss.
    5. Repeat at every shoe-moment this week — on, off, on — and let the routine do the hundreds of repetitions for you.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card is a simple shoe, plain and easy to read. The part worth watching happens below the waist: say the word near your baby’s feet and see whether a kick or a wriggle answers. Feet respond early at this age, and the shoe-word is one of the few words aimed straight at them.

    Ask your child

    Watch the doorway: does your baby’s attention come to the shoe as it goes on, or to your face? Does the word alone start to mean “outside is happening”? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you like the going-out shoe or the coming-home shoe better.”

    What your child can say or do

    A foot-kick at the word, watching the shoe’s approach with total focus, grabbing for the strap mid-fitting, or a full-body wriggle of excitement at the door — shoe moments are high-information moments, and your baby is fluent in all of them.

    Out in the real world

    Shoe-moments run the week: the door mat, the car seat, the pushchair basket, the pile by grandma’s door. Every one is a repetition of this card — and unlike most vocabulary, this word’s rehearsals are scheduled by life itself.

    Try it together

    Feet hello: at nappy changes, touch each sock and say “sock”, then hold the shoe near and say “shoe”. Three seconds, twice a day. The feet become a named country, and your baby is its most attentive cartographer.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did a real shoe get its word at a real doorway today, and did the card-to-foot link happen at least once? The body connection is what separates this word from a picture — shoes live on feet, and feet live on your baby.

    Parent tips

    Say the word at the calmest shoe-moment of the day, not the rushed one — words said in hurry carry hurry. If your baby grabs for shoes constantly, that is stage-typical exploration: the named shoe is the chewed shoe; wash, repeat, continue.

    Staying safe

    Shoes off for sleep and never a plaything in the cot — street shoes track in what streets track. Keep the fitting calm: a wiggly foot plus a distracted grown-up is how little toes get squeezed, and the word should always predict a kind shoe.

    This lesson pairs with the Shoe flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

    Cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Your baby has met this word before, in the Infant sets — and meeting it again is not repetition but reinforcement: the spine of a first vocabulary is built from returns. This time, there is a new twist: hands.

    What is this?

    A cup is the everyday drinking vessel your baby has seen at every feed of their life. In the earlier sets it was a word to hear; now, at 6–9 months, it is an object to hold — and holding changes what the word can mean.

    What does it mean?

    Memory works by returns: each re-meeting of a word in a new set, at a new ability level, deepens it. The grip is the new ingredient — your baby can now grasp the real cup themselves, which turns cup from a watched thing into a handled one.

    What does the child need to know?

    The upgrade is in the hands: during the card moment, put a real baby cup into your baby’s grip and say the word as they hold it. Holding and naming go together now. The word has not changed — your baby has, and the card is here to prove it.

    Why this matters

    Repeated words across sets are the architecture of vocabulary, not a flaw in the plan: cup heard at 3 months, held at 7 months, drunk from at 12 — each stage files the word deeper. This lesson is the holding instalment of a word your child will use for life.

    What it teaches

    Grasp-and-hold coordination, word-object mapping through touch, two-handed handling, and the satisfaction of holding the very thing the card shows.

    Words to learn

    cupholdgriptwo handsdrinkmine

    Say this to your child

    ““Cup! Here is the picture cup. And now — here is a real one, just for your hands. Hold it! Feel how it goes — one hand, two hands, up and down. You are holding your cup. The same word as the picture, right there in your fingers.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at viewing distance: “Cup! You know this one — you have known it for ages.”
    2. Trace the cup’s shape, then tap the card twice — old friends get a warm greeting.
    3. Fetch a real baby cup — light, clean, cool — and hold it out towards your baby’s hands.
    4. As their grip lands, say “cup” once. Let them hold it as long as they like: turning it, chewing the handle, banging it gently.
    5. End with the card and a summary line — “you held your cup!” — then let the real cup join ordinary playtime, where it belongs.

    Look closer at the picture

    The picture is a plain everyday cup, drawn simply and clearly. Once a real cup is in your baby’s hands, watch the handling science begin: swapping from hand to hand, banging, investigating the handle with their mouth. Every one of those experiments is exactly right for this stage — and the word cup goes with each attempt.

    Ask your child

    Watch the grip: is the hold steady now, or still tetchy? Does your baby look from the real cup to the card, checking that they match? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if holding it makes the word bigger in your head. It should — that is how this works.”

    What your child can say or do

    A firm two-handed grip, hand-switching practice, a proud bang on the tray, or the cup raised vaguely towards the mouth — drinking is months away from masterful, but the aimed lift is the milestone, and the word is riding on it.

    Out in the real world

    Cups keep appearing all day: at meals, in the bath, in other people’s hands. With holding now in your baby’s skill set, every sighting can become a holding attempt — which is exactly the trajectory this card is feeding.

    Try it together

    Pass-it-back: hand your baby the cup, hold out your palm, and let them give it back — then again. Giving and taking is the social side of handling, and it rehearses the turn-taking that all conversation, someday, will run on.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the real cup actually get held today, and did the word arrive at the moment of the grip? Timing is everything here — the word must land on the holding, not float near it.

    Parent tips

    If your baby would rather bang than hold, that is holding too, at this age — banging is handling with rhythm. Do not chase drinking skills; the cup-card lesson is about the word and the grip, and both are already working.

    Staying safe

    The holding cup is a baby cup: unbreakable, cool, empty or with water only — never hot, never full to the brim, never the sharp-edged family china. Chewing the handle is expected; check the cup for bite-marks before its next shift.

    This lesson pairs with the Cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

    Spoon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    No other card gets so many live performances — meals run several times a day, and the spoon always stars. This lesson adds the newest trick: the handover.

    What is this?

    A spoon is the mealtime scoop your baby has watched working since their first week. At 6–9 months their hands have caught up with their interest: they can grab, hold and wave the real thing. The card names the tool; the handover makes it theirs.

    What does it mean?

    The grab is understanding in action: a baby who snatches the spoon as it is offered has linked the word, the object and their own power to take it. Language plus motor skill arriving at the same moment — that is what this stage is for.

    What does the child need to know?

    The handover is the lesson: at mealtime, offer the spoon handle-first into your baby’s reaching hand and say the word as their fingers close. The card prepares the name; the meal supplies the grab. Say it once — the taking is loud enough on its own.

    Why this matters

    Meals give this word a stage several times a day, which no other card can match. And the spoon is destined to matter: in the coming months it becomes your baby’s own tool, and every self-fed bite will rest on the word-and-grasp partnership built here.

    What it teaches

    Reaching and grasping on request, tool recognition, hand-to-mouth journeys (self-feeding’s first drafts), and word-action pairing at real events.

    Words to learn

    spoongrabholdscoopmoreall done

    Say this to your child

    ““Spoon! Here is the picture spoon, long and shiny. And here — take it! This is your very own spoon, handle first. Grab, hold, wave — that is exactly right. The spoon brings the food, and now it knows your hands. Best tool in the kitchen.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at viewing distance: “Spoon! The busiest word in the kitchen.”
    2. Trace the bowl and the handle — this is a tool, and tools have parts worth knowing.
    3. At the next meal, offer a real spoon handle-first into your baby’s reach, saying “spoon” as they take it.
    4. Let the spoon be theirs for a minute — waved, gummed, bashed on the tray — then reclaim it calmly for the eating it came to do.
    5. Repeat the handover daily; within weeks the reach will start before the word finishes.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a shiny spoon, simple and clear — say that much. The live noticing: does the reach come before the word finishes, or after? Timing the reach against the word, week by week, is watching anticipation turn into understanding.

    Ask your child

    Watch the taking: does your baby’s grip aim for the handle or the bowl? Do they wave it or head straight for the mouth? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you think the spoon is yours now. I have news for you — eventually it will be.”

    What your child can say or do

    A swift two-hand snatch, triumphant spoon-waving, gumming the handle with total commitment, or the spoon banged on the tray like a tiny drum — all of it is tool-familiarity, and every grab is your baby voting for self-feeding months early.

    Out in the real world

    Spoon moments happen at every meal: yours, theirs, the serving spoon, the little weaning set. With grabbing now online, each meal can carry one handover — the most-repeated lesson in the whole collection, served daily with lunch.

    Try it together

    Spoon ferry: hand the spoon over, open your palm, and let your baby give it back; then hand it over again. Three or four crossings. The ferry game builds voluntary release — harder than grabbing, and the social glue of every exchange to come.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the handover happen at a real meal today, and did the word land exactly on the grab? Precision beats frequency here — one perfectly-timed word teaches more than twenty that miss the moment.

    Parent tips

    If your baby grabs for the card instead, let the card be held too — then bring the real spoon in as the upgrade. Do not fight the gumming; the mouth is this age’s second pair of hands, and the spoon survives it.

    Staying safe

    The handed-over spoon is the baby’s own — soft-tipped, unbreakable, sized for small fists. Hot or loaded spoons stay with you; the handover happens with the clean starter spoon, before the messy course begins.

    This lesson pairs with the Spoon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

    Car — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Cars whoosh past windows and car parks all day, and few words get rehearsed so generously by the world itself. This lesson flies the card, parks it, and names the traffic.

    What is this?

    A car is a wheeled machine that carries people — fast, bright, endlessly passing. The card gives one a portrait; your hand gives it a slow flight across your baby’s view; the window supplies the real fleet, free of charge.

    What does it mean?

    A slow pass is better than a fast one at this stage: your baby’s tracking can now follow something quite quick, but comprehension lives in the slow. And the parking — the card landing to rest — is a concept worth naming: rides end, engines stop, things arrive.

    What does the child need to know?

    Fly the card in one slow pass across the view, then park it deliberately on your lap and say so: parked. Later, at any window, name the real cars — one word per pass, not per minute. Watch for your baby tracking real cars outside; that look is this card, alive.

    Why this matters

    Car is a word your baby will hear for the rest of their life, several times a day, in every country and language on earth. Building the picture-sound-word package now means every future sighting lands on an old friend — few words repay their lesson so often.

    What it teaches

    Smooth tracking of slow and fast passes, event naming in real time, the parking concept (movement has endings), and visual attention out at distance.

    Words to learn

    carvroomslowfastparkstop

    Say this to your child

    ““Car! Watch it go — vroom, across the sky... and park. See? The car stopped right here on my knee. Rides always end somewhere. And look outside — more cars! Going past, one after another. Each one is the same word: car.””

    Step by step

    1. Bring the card up and open the show: “Car! Ready to drive.”
    2. Fly it in one slow, level pass across your baby’s view, left to right, with a soft vroom at the end.
    3. Land it gently on your lap and name the landing: “Parked. The car stopped.” Then lift off again if the eyes ask for more.
    4. At the window or on a walk, name real cars one at a time as they pass — word per event, not per minute.
    5. End with the card parked, so the session itself has a proper stopping place.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a speedy little car — say that much. The live noticing: does your baby’s gaze stay with the slow pass all the way, and does the parking earn a look? The stop is the underrated half — movement is easy to watch; endings have to be learned.

    Ask your child

    Watch the pass: fast or slow today — which holds better? Does your baby look back to the parked card, hoping for another flight? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you are waiting for the vroom now. I think you know it is coming.”

    What your child can say or do

    Smooth head-tracking through the whole pass, a bounce at the vroom, eyes returning to the lap for the restart, or a head-turn at real engines outside — the last one is the word escaping into the wild, which is where every card eventually wants to live.

    Out in the real world

    Cars never stop coming: the street outside, the car park, the drive home, the delivery van. Naming real traffic one car at a time is the world’s most generous vocabulary drill, and your baby is enrolled in it permanently.

    Try it together

    Red-light game: fly the card, then stop it mid-air — “red light, stop!” — hold, then release — “green light, go!” The stop-and-go is object permanence plus cause-and-effect with wheels on, and it becomes a toddler car-game later. Plant it now.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the pass actually run slow today, and did the parking get named? Fast is flashy, slow is learnable — and the named stop is the concept most parents forget to teach, which makes it the most valuable half of this lesson.

    Parent tips

    Vary pass direction and height across days; predictable is boring for the thrower, unpredictable is rich for the watcher. If real cars outside outshine the card, follow the stare — the card taught the word, the street gets to perform it.

    Staying safe

    Traffic naming happens from the pushchair or your arms, well back from the road edge — the lesson is at windows and pavements, never driveways. Card flights stay indoors; paper does not belong in car parks.

    This lesson pairs with the Car flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & EVERYDAY OBJECTS · AGES 6–9 MONTHS

    Teddy bear — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The last card of the Baby 1 stage names, for many families, a real resident: the bear on the shelf, the hugged, gummed, dragged-everywhere friend. This lesson gives that friend a formal role.

    What is this?

    A teddy bear is a soft toy companion — and at 6–9 months, a baby can reach for it, clutch it and make it part of every game. The card is the friend’s portrait; the session makes the friend a participant.

    What does it mean?

    A comfort object in the routine does double duty: it holds the word (teddy) and it holds the feeling (safe). Babies this age are building attachment structures as fast as they build vocabulary, and the two builds share the same scaffolding.

    What does the child need to know?

    Bring the real bear to meet the card, then hand over a promotion: from now on, teddy picks which card comes next — your hand operates the paw. When a comfort object joins the routine, sessions often stretch happily longer. Follow that warmth wherever it goes.

    Why this matters

    Ending this stage with the warmest word is good sequencing: the set closes on security, not novelty. Babies who finish card time with their friend beside them file the whole ritual under good things — and good things get requested, reached for, and remembered.

    What it teaches

    Attachment behaviour (reaching for the comfort object), word-object mapping for a beloved thing, social ritual-building, and the reach-and-clutch skills that teddy makes worth practising.

    Words to learn

    teddybearsoftfriendpickcuddle

    Say this to your child

    ““Teddy bear! Here is the picture bear — and here is YOUR bear, come to sit with us. Hold on tight. Now watch: teddy gets to choose our next card. What will it be? Teddy says... this one! A very good choice, teddy. You are part of the class now.””

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and greet it like a mutual acquaintance: “Teddy bear! I think you two know each other.”
    2. Fetch the real bear and bring it face to face with the card, letting your baby look between them.
    3. Offer the real bear into your baby’s reach — at this age they can clutch it themselves, and will.
    4. Give teddy its new job: the paw taps the next card, your voice announces the choice, and the session continues under new management.
    5. Close with teddy present and the cards away — the friend attends the whole class from now on.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a soft teddy bear in the set’s realistic-friendly style — say that much. The live noticing: does your baby clutch the bear unprompted, and do their eyes run the triangle — card bear, real bear, your face? The triangle is attachment and vocabulary sharing one loop.

    Ask your child

    Watch the attachment: does the bear get sought out at session time now, before the cards even appear? Does the word alone collect a look towards the shelf? Wonder aloud: “I wonder if you think the card bear and the shelf bear are the same bear. Honestly — so do I.”

    What your child can say or do

    An immediate grab-and-clutch of the real bear, dragging it close against the chest, eyes swinging between the two bears, or babbling happily at the teddy-voice — and eventually, the reach towards the bear when the word is said. That reach is the word, arriving.

    Out in the real world

    Teddy keeps a fuller diary than anyone: the cot, the pram, the car seat, grandma’s, the washing line. Each appearance is a replay — and from this week, each appearance can also include a naming by your baby’s own reach: the bear they fetch is the word they know.

    Try it together

    Teddy picks, extended: let the paw choose which two cards face off, and name the winner with drama — “teddy chose... the dog!” The selection ceremony makes your baby a spectator at a game with stakes, which is the most attention-compelling format there is.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the bear get promoted today — from prop to participant — and did the session actually run warmer with them present? If yes, keep the promotion permanent; the ritual is doing more work than any single card in the set.

    Parent tips

    If your family runs no comfort object, this card still teaches a beloved animal-word — borrow the nearest plush and promote them instead. Keep the teddy-voice stable across weeks; your baby is mapping that voice to the word as surely as to the fur.

    Staying safe

    The promoted bear passes the baby-safety check: embroidered features, no small parts, nothing shedding, washed sometimes. Cot-sleep rules stay theirs — the bear’s new job is card time, and the two roles never have to merge.

    This lesson pairs with the Teddy bear flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Everyday Objects (Baby 1).
